Overview: mChatAI+ is a native macOS app that goes well beyond a chat window. It's a complete AI workspace that runs on your own machine, with your own API keys, combining things most setups force you to glue together yourself:
A chat surface that talks to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, Perplexity, Ollama, Apple's on-device Foundation model, and more — switched from one menu.
Forty applets covering writing, audio, reading, maps, presentations, structured data, video and images. See the feature showcase for all of them, with screenshots.

Overview: A visual automation engine — Pipelines, Skills, and a DAG canvas — for chaining AI calls, web fetches, file operations and scripts into workflows you can rerun.
An AI Harness that plans, builds, evaluates and installs working mini-apps and games from a sentence.
An agent portal, so Claude Code or Codex can drive the app from your terminal — open an applet, write a document, build a deck, query your data.

text:
Overview — Two strong defaults: Bring your own keys. Every LLM call uses your API key by default, and the fully local path — Apple's Foundation model or Ollama — is always available.
Your work stays on your machine. Documents, recordings, pipelines, custom skills and microservices all run and live locally. The platform never deploys your code centrally.

Overview — Where to start: New to the app? Getting started is the shortest path to something useful.
Want to see what it does first? The feature showcase has a page per applet.
Ready to install? Downloads & install.
Getting started: Once mChatAI+ is installed (see Downloads & install), here's the shortest path to something useful.

Getting started — 1. Pick a model — or don't: You can start with no API key at all. In Chat, choose Foundation from the provider menu and everything runs on your Mac using Apple's on-device model.
For the stronger models, open Settings → LLM Providers and paste a key. mChatAI+ supports Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, Perplexity, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, and Ollama (local, no key needed). Keys are stored in your macOS Keychain. Providers you haven't configured stay hidden from the picker.

Getting started — 2. Set up your home screen: The home screen groups applets into bands. Right-click any tile to move it into Core or push it down to More Apps. If you want to see everything the app ships with, turn on Show Experimental — that reveals ten more applets including ToonStudio, LoopStar and Vault.

Getting started — 3. Ask the AI Harness for something: Open AI Harness and describe what you want: *"a calm 3-minute breathing mini-app with a pulsing circle,"* or *"a tip calculator that splits the bill,"* or *"a poker game with two AI opponents."* It plans, generates, evaluates and installs the result so you can use it straight away. Full macOS apps need mChatAIShell installed for the build step.

Getting started — 4. Run a pipeline: Go to AI Automation → Pipelines and run one of the bundled templates. Each is a small chain of skills you can clone, tweak and rerun, with every step shown executing live.

Getting started — 5. Point your terminal at it: If you already use Claude Code or Codex, mChatAI+ can be driven from there — open an applet, write a document, build a slide deck, read your Ledger tables. See Developer tools.
Not sure where to start? The feature showcase has a screenshot and a "how to try it" for every applet.

Downloads & install — mChatAI+ for macOS: Get it on the Mac App Store (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mchatai/id6757826624?mt=12) — the normal way to install. Requires macOS 15.5 or later.
There's also a direct download: the same app, signed for direct distribution, for when you need a fix that's still in App Store review.

Downloads & install — mChatAI for iOS: Get it on the App Store (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mchatai/id6445939409?platform=iphone). Chats, AI ToDo lists, AI Write documents and MapGuide tours sync between the two apps over iCloud.

Downloads & install — mChatAI for Android: Get it on Google Play (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sevenhillsstudio.mchatai). Chat, the Community Hub, audio, radio, news, the reader and Map Guide. It does not sync with the Apple apps — those sync over iCloud, which Android cannot read — so tours and mini-apps travel between them through the Community Hub instead.

Downloads & install — mChatAIShell — companion helper: mChatAIShell is a small menu-bar helper that lets mChatAI+ build apps and run scripts on your machine. You only need it for:
Building full macOS apps with AI Harness
Running the Python microservices some recipes use
Skills that need your filesystem or local tools like git
When mChatAI+ needs it for something you've asked for, it walks you through the install.

mChatAIShell: mChatAIShell is a small companion app for macOS that runs alongside mChatAI+. It lives in your menu bar and lets mChatAI+ do things on your machine that the main app — running inside Apple's App Sandbox — can't do on its own.
You only need it if you want one of these capabilities. Otherwise, mChatAI+ runs fine without it.

keywords: building macos apps from ai harness.
text:
mChatAIShell — What it unlocks: Building macOS apps from AI Harness. Without the shell, the harness can build web mini-apps. With the shell installed, it can also build full native macOS apps.
Python microservices. Some recipes (icon generation, image processing, mail handling, etc.) run as small Python services on your machine. The shell installs and runs them for you.
Filesystem and shell skills. Skills that need access to files outside the sandbox, or that need to run common tools like git, only work when the shell is running.

mChatAIShell — How it works: When you install mChatAIShell, an icon appears in your menu bar. Click it for a small popover with four tabs:
Status — connection state, the code that authorizes mChatAI+ to talk to it, and overall health.
Capabilities — which local tools (Python, Node, GitHub CLI, etc.) are installed and ready, with one-click install for anything missing.
Activity — a log of what mChatAI+ has asked the shell to do recently.
Permissions — which API keys it's been authorized to read from your macOS Keychain.
mChatAIShell — How it works: mChatAIShell registers itself as a login item, so after the first launch it auto-starts every time you log in. You can quit it any time from its menu-bar popover.

mChatAIShell — How to install it: Download the .dmg from mchatai.com/macos (https://mchatai.com/macos) and drag mChatAIShell into Applications.
Launch it once. The menu-bar icon appears.
Open the menu-bar popover, copy the authorization code, and paste it into mChatAI+ → Settings → Shell Bridge.
The first time mChatAIShell needs to read an API key from your Keychain, macOS will prompt for permission. Allow it once and it remembers.
That's the whole setup. From then on mChatAI+ uses the shell automatically whenever a skill or harness build needs it.

mChatAIShell — Privacy: mChatAIShell only listens on your own machine. Nothing on the network outside your laptop can talk to it.
API keys stay in your macOS Keychain. The shell reads them when needed; it doesn't copy them anywhere else.
The app is signed and notarized by Apple.

Pipelines: A pipeline is a sequence of steps. Each step is a skill — webSearch, llmGenerate, readFile, ttsRender, anything in the skill catalog — and each step's output flows into the next step's input. You build them visually, save them as templates, run them on demand, or schedule them.

Pipelines — Why pipelines are the centerpiece: Most agentic frameworks expose only two ends of the spectrum: a single LLM call, or a fully autonomous agent. Pipelines are the middle. They're deterministic where you want determinism (fetch this URL, write this file), and they delegate to an LLM only where judgment is actually required. That makes them debuggable, cheap, repeatable, and trustable.
A pipeline can:
Pull data from an API or scrape a webpage
Transform it with a deterministic skill (JSON parse, regex, dedupe)
Hand the result to an LLM for summarization or classification
Validate the LLM's output with another LLM step
Pipelines — Why pipelines are the centerpiece: Save the result, post it to your AI Feed, render it as audio, or chain into another pipeline

Pipelines — Building one: In AI Automation → Pipelines:
New Pipeline — name it, pick an icon.
Add steps — each row is a step. Pick a skill, configure it, drag to reorder.
Run — the right pane streams progress per step. You can rerun from any step.
Save as template if you want to share it or run it on a schedule.
Pipelines — Templates that ship in the box: The app bundles starter pipelines under AI Automation → Templates. They're meant to be cloned and modified.

Skills: A skill is a single, well-defined operation. Pipelines and agents compose skills. They come from three places:
Built-in skills — shipped in the app. The fastest, most reliable.
JavaScript skills — you can write your own in SkillForge (the in-app editor) or install ones from the Community Hub.
Provider templates — pre-built wrappers for common API patterns. Configure a few fields and you have a working skill.

Skills — What's in the catalog: The built-in catalog covers file and text operations, LLM calls, web search and fetch, media (TTS, image, audio), and integrations with common APIs. Some skills require mChatAIShell for access to your local filesystem and shell tools.
Open AI Automation → Skills for the live list with descriptions, configuration options, and example invocations.

Skills — Writing your own: SkillForge is the in-app skill builder. Describe what you want, SkillForge scaffolds the JavaScript, you test it inside the editor, save it, and it's instantly available to every pipeline and agent. Sharing is opt-in — your skill stays on your machine unless you publish it.

Agents: Where a pipeline is a fixed sequence, an agent decides what to do next on its own. It plans, executes a skill, evaluates the result, and decides whether it's done or needs to keep going.
Agents are useful when the path to the goal isn't known up front — research, exploration, multi-step assistant work. They're more expensive than pipelines (more LLM calls, more variance), so the pattern is: start with a pipeline, escalate to an agent only when you actually need the open-endedness.

Agents — What you can see: The agent surface shows you the things most frameworks hide:
Inner monologue — the agent's planning text, not a summary.
Tool calls — every skill invocation with its config and result.
Reflection — periodic self-checks against the goal.
Cost — running token + dollar count.

Agents — Safety gates: Approval gates — for write operations (sending email, posting, creating files), the agent stops and asks before executing.
Termination guards — a hard cap on turns plus a "no measurable progress" detector. No agent runs forever; stuck agents auto-cancel.
Tool whitelists — agents only see the skills you grant them. Risky skills are opt-in, not on by default.

Agents — Built-in agents: Research Agent — multi-source research with citation tracking.
You can also build your own from AI Automation → Agents.

AI Harness: AI Harness turns a plain-English idea into a working artifact — a web mini-app, a game, a macOS app, a Python microservice. You describe what you want, and the harness plans, generates, evaluates, optionally iterates, and installs the result.
You find it in AI Automation → Harness.

AI Harness — How it works: Plan — pick the right approach for what you asked for.
Generate — write the code.
Evaluate — run the artifact and check it works.
Auto-fix — if evaluation flags something concrete, patch it and retry.
Install — once the result passes, the harness installs it and offers to publish to the Community Hub.

AI Harness — Iteration: After the first turn you can keep going: *"add a high-score table,"* *"make the cards bigger on mobile,"* *"swap to a dark theme."* Follow-up turns ship a small patch over the installed artifact instead of regenerating the whole thing — fast, cheap, and non-destructive.

AI Harness — What needs mChatAIShell: Web mini-apps and games run inside mChatAI+ — no extra install needed. macOS apps and Python microservices need mChatAIShell (the companion helper) so the harness can run a build on your machine.
Mini Apps: Mini Apps are small HTML/JS/CSS applications that run inside mChatAI+. They're the fastest way to go from an idea to something playable — and they're the most common output of AI Harness.

Mini Apps — How they get there: Three paths:
Bundled — a small set ship with the app for first-launch.
AI Harness — describe one, the harness builds and installs it locally. No publishing required.
Community Hub — browse mini-apps other people published at mchatai.com/hub (https://mchatai.com/hub) and install with one click.

Mini Apps — Publishing to the Community Hub: When you build a mini-app you like, Publish to Community Hub uploads a playable copy for review. After it passes automated checks and moderation approval, it can appear on mchatai.com so other users can play it in their browser or install it into their own mChatAI+.
Your submitted items remain visible to you in the app while they are waiting for review. Public Hub listings are limited to approved items, and every public item includes reporting tools so users can flag copyright, safety, spam, or other issues.

Applets: Applets are the surfaces inside mChatAI+ — the things you actually spend time in. There are 40. Each is built on the same shared foundation (skills, pipelines, agents, the artifact store), so output from one becomes input to another: a LoopStar jingle lands in the Audio Library, a Ledger table becomes a live chart in an AI Slides deck, an agent's research is written into an AI Write document.
Browse the full showcase → — a page per applet, with a screenshot, what it does, and how to try it.

Applets — How the home screen is organised: Applets are grouped into bands you can rearrange:
| Band | What's in it |
|------|--------------|
| Core | The five you use most.

Applets — How the home screen is organised: Chat, AI Write, Hands Free AI, Hub and AI Automation by default — right-click any tile to promote or demote it. |
| Audio | AI Audio, AI Music, Audio Books, Podcasts, Audiocast Creator, Audio Script Creator. |
| Knowledge | AI Web, AI Reader, Wikipedia, AI News, AI Radio, Quiznect. |
| Tools | AI ToDo, MapGuide, AI Weather, AI Calendar, AI Contacts, DreamSnap, StoryMaker, Video Recorder, AI Slides. |
| Platform | For You, AI Feed, Ledger, AI Harness — the parts that tie everything else together. |
| More Apps | Collapsed by default.

Applets — How the home screen is organised: A fresh install parks AI ToDo, Wikipedia, AI Weather, AI Calendar, AI Contacts, StoryMaker and Quiznect here, and anything you demote joins them. |
| Experimental | Hidden until you switch Show Experimental on. Ten applets live here, including ToonStudio, LoopStar, Vault and Image Studio. |

Applets — Applets an agent can drive: Fourteen applets expose named commands that Claude Code, Codex or any agent connected through the CLI portal can call directly — LoopStar, MapGuide, AI Audio, AI Write, AI Slides, AI ToDo, Ledger, Hub, AI Web, DreamSnap, AI News, and the cross-applet asset and workbench surfaces. Each applet's page in the showcase lists its commands.

LLM providers: mChatAI+ talks to many LLM providers from a single picker. Add a key once in Settings → LLM Providers and that provider's full model catalog becomes available everywhere — chat, pipelines, agents, wizard.

LLM providers — Supported providers: mChatAI+ supports Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, Perplexity, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, and Ollama (fully local — no API key needed).
For each provider, the picker exposes the latest models that provider publishes. Open the model picker inside mChatAI+ for the current list — model lineups change often.
LLM providers — Cost visibility: Every LLM call records token counts and cost so you can see what's actually expensive and tune it.
Recipes: Recipes are pre-built use cases — known-good combinations of pipelines, skills, and prompts you can run with one click.

Recipes — Tiers (by how much setup they need): | Tier | What's needed |
|------|---------------|
| Tier 0 | Nothing — run immediately |
| Tier 1 | At least one LLM API key |
| Tier 2 | LLM key plus a specific provider API key (Gmail, GitHub, etc.) |
| Tier 3 | mChatAIShell installed |

Recipes — Where to find them: Inside mChatAI+:
AI Automation → Templates lists pipeline recipes with their tier badge and setup steps.
AI Automation → Recipes lists harness-buildable artifacts (games, mini-apps, microservices) with example prompts.
Recipes — Adding your own: Any pipeline you build can be saved as a template. Any mini-app you generate can be published to the Community Hub.

Features: mChatAI+ ships 40 applets. Every one below has its own page with a screenshot, what it actually does, and how to try it.
Open the visual showcase →

AI Automation: Describe what you want built and it builds it, or wire skills together on a canvas yourself.
Everyday · On the home screen by default

AI Automation — What it does: Opens on the Harness tab, where you type into a box that reads 'Describe what you want to make or automate...' and the app builds it. The code defines fourteen kinds of thing it can aim at, including Pipeline, DAG Pipeline, AI Agent, Custom Skill, MCP Server, Python Service, Mini App, macOS App, Widget, Browser Test, Full-Stack App and Unity Game.

AI Automation — What it does: Shows the work in three panes: a sessions sidebar with a 'New AI Automation' button and a 'Products' section that counts finished results; the conversation in the middle; and a right-hand pane with Preview, Logs, Terminal and Files tabs. While a run is going you can type a steering message — it shows as 'Steering queued — will redirect after current step' and can be cancelled without stopping the run — or press Stop.

AI Automation — What it does: Keeps web mini-app versions honest: a version chip in the preview header, a 'Version History' popover that lists each build with Open and Rollback, and an 'Iterate' button that branches a clean new numbered version so the original stays untouched.
Has a Pipelines tab with three sub-tabs — Canvas, Recipes and Community Hub. On the canvas you right-click to 'Add Skill...' or 'Add Flow Control...', connect and configure nodes, and press the play button ('Save & Run pipeline'). A side chat drafts a pipeline from plain language and offers Load, Save and Save & Run.

AI Automation — What it does: Has a Skills tab (Skill Forge) that generates a JavaScript skill from a description, tests it against input you supply, loops an AI QA pass over it for 1 to 6 attempts, and then installs it.

AI Automation — What it does: Rounds out with a Workbench tab that runs a command-line coding agent inside the app (live permission-mode and model menus, Stop/Resume, a per-session cost readout, and a choice of the real interactive terminal or a structured chat), a Services tab that schedules pipelines, agents and web watches on eight cadences from every 5 minutes to monthly, and Agents, Monitor, Packs, System (Memory / Storage / Quality / Security) and Setup (Configuration, External APIs, Local Tools, Shell & Services, MCP, Multi-Platform) tabs.

AI Automation — How to try it: On the home screen, click the AI Automation tile. It opens on the Harness tab.
Type what you want into the box that reads 'Describe what you want to make or automate...' and press Return.
Watch the run in the middle pane; the right-hand pane previews the result, and finished work is listed under 'Products' in the sidebar.
To build something by hand instead, click the Pipelines tab, right-click the canvas and choose 'Add Skill...', then press the play button to save and run it.

AI Automation — Works with: Hub — a 'Community Hub' sub-tab sits inside the Pipelines tab filtered to pipelines, and its 'Open in AIHarness' button hands a published item back to the Harness to branch
mChatAIShell, the separate companion app — the Harness shows a banner when the session's artifact type requires the shell (macOS app build, Python service, full-stack deploy) and the shell isn't connected
Command-line coding agents — the Workbench's Agent picker offers claude, codex and gemini, with availability decided by content config rather than hardcoded
AI Automation — Works with: Ledger — the Workbench header has an 'Open the source Ledger this was built from' button on results built from Ledger data

AI Write: A document editor with ten one-click AI edits: fix grammar, adjust tone, simplify, summarize, expand.
Everyday · On the home screen by default

AI Write — What it does: Is a real document editor first: a sidebar list of documents with live word counts, a title field, undo/redo, a text-size stepper, and an autosave that fires about a second and a half after you stop typing.
Offers ten AI operations from the sparkles button in the toolbar — Fix Grammar, Improve Style, Adjust Tone, Rewrite, Summarize, Expand, Simplify, Format & Clean Up, Extract Action Items, Key Quotes. 'Adjust Tone' opens a sheet where you type the tone you want (pre-filled with 'professional').

AI Write — What it does: Never overwrites your draft behind your back: the result lands in a panel at the bottom of the editor with Accept / Copy / Dismiss. Accept replaces the document text; Dismiss leaves the original alone. Every operation is passed the whole document, not a selection.
Dictates straight into the document: a 'Dictate' button records, and a separate menu chooses whether speech-to-text runs on-device or through OpenAI or Google.
Renders Markdown. A document that reads as Markdown opens rendered, and a Preview/Edit button (Shift-Cmd-P) flips between the rendered page and the raw source.

AI Write — What it does: Carries a second, separate 'AI Actions' popover (the cpu button) with five prompt-driven actions — Summarize, Expand, Rewrite, Extract Key Points and Translate — whose result gets the same Accept / Copy / Dismiss panel.

AI Write — How to try it: On the home screen, click the AI Write tile.
Click the + button beside 'Documents' in the sidebar, then type or paste a draft into the editor.
Click the sparkles button in the editor toolbar and choose 'Fix Grammar' (or 'Summarize', 'Adjust Tone', and so on).
Read the result in the panel that appears at the bottom and click 'Accept' to replace your draft, or 'Dismiss' to keep it as it was.

AI Write — Works with: The agent layer — four verbs (listDocs, getDoc, createDoc, appendDoc) reach the same document store the window reads, so an agent's research or report can be written straight into AI Write
The artifact router — AIWriteIngestHandler is registered for Markdown documents, research reports and blog posts, so output produced elsewhere in the app can be filed here as a document
The iOS mChatAI app — both apps' AI Write stores are wired to the same CloudKit record type, so documents are meant to appear on both

Chat: One chat window for every model you've set up; it can search the web or read a project folder first.
Everyday · On the home screen by default

Chat — What it does: Puts one chat window in front of eight back ends — Apple's on-device Foundation model, Ollama, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, OpenRouter and mChatAI Cloud — picked from a menu at the top left. The menu hides any provider you have not configured: cloud providers need a stored API key, Ollama only appears when Ollama is actually reachable on your machine, and mChatAI Cloud only when a feature flag is on. Right-clicking an assistant reply opens 'Show details' with cost in USD, input/output token counts, model, provider and a copy-able generation id — each section shown only when the provider reported those numbers.

Chat — What it does: Keeps conversations in a left sidebar, saved as one JSON file per conversation and written to iCloud (CloudKit) when it is available, with a manual 'Sync with iCloud' button as well. A pencil button starts a new thread, right-click deletes one, and a gear menu offers 'Delete All Conversations'. Runs made by the AI Harness are filtered out so they never appear in the list.

Chat — What it does: Switches the assistant's character with a persona menu at the top of the window — General Assistant, The Comedian, Fitness Coach, The Chef, The Historian and Life Coach ship built in. A button next to it opens a manager where you add your own persona and write its System Prompt.
Attaches files with the paperclip: the app extracts their text and prepends it as context, capped at 20,000 characters. For Anthropic and Google it sends PDFs and text files to the model as native document attachments rather than flattening them, and sends images inline where the provider supports it.

Chat — What it does: Adds live web context when you turn on the globe button. The model you already selected is first asked, in a short JSON-only call, whether the question needs current information; if it says yes the app searches DuckDuckGo, takes up to five results, reads the first two pages (about 2,000 characters each) and shows the sources as clickable chips. Clicking a chip opens an in-app browser sheet instead of jumping to Safari.

Chat — What it does: Searches a code folder you point it at with the folder button: the model proposes filenames to open and grep terms to look for, the app does the reading and grepping locally, and only the matching excerpts go back to the model.

Chat — How to try it: On the home screen, click the Chat tile.
Pick a model from the provider menu at the top left of the chat window — 'Foundation' runs on your Mac and needs no API key.
Type into the box that reads 'Type or speak...' and press Return (Shift+Return for a new line).
Click the globe button and ask about something recent — the pages it read appear as source chips above the composer.

Chat — Works with: AI Audio — when the selected model is a music model (an id containing lyria, suno, riffusion, songbloom or musicgen) the request generates a track, saves it to the Audio Library's Generated folder and posts an inline player in the chat
Hands Free AI — it builds the same ChatViewModel and the same PersonaManager, so it is literally the same chat engine driven by voice
Ollama — local models appear in the same provider menu, and the code marks Foundation and Ollama as running on the user's own machine

Hands Free AI: Dictate long-form into a transcript you can edit, then send the whole thing to the chat at once.
Everyday · On the home screen by default · Asks for Microphone permission the first time

Hands Free AI — What it does: Records continuously into a transcript that keeps growing, rather than doing one short dictation at a time. A large 'Start Recording' / 'Stop Recording' button and a running timer sit in the left sidebar.

AI Calendar: Your Apple Calendar in a day or week view, with a sidebar where you type an event in plain English.
Tools · Asks for Calendar permission the first time

AI Calendar — What it does: Shows your Apple Calendar events two ways: Day lists that day's events as cards, Week draws seven columns. Events are re-fetched through EventKit whenever you switch view or step forward and back.
Type a request into the "Scheduling AI" sidebar and a model returns a title, start, end and notes, which are saved as a new event on your default Apple Calendar. Your existing events are included in the prompt, so asking for a free slot tells the model to avoid overlaps.

AI Calendar — What it does: A "Schedule Insight" panel asks a model to read the loaded events, plus any overlapping pairs the app worked out, and reply with two or three sentences of suggestions.
The "+" toolbar button opens a "New Event" sheet: Event Title, an "All Day" toggle, Start and End date pickers, and optional notes.
Clicking an event card opens a detail sheet with the date, time, duration in minutes, calendar name, location, notes, and a "Join Zoom" / "Join Google Meet" / "Join Teams" / "Join Webex" link pulled out of the event's URL, location or notes.

AI Calendar — How to try it: On the home screen, expand the "More Apps" band and click the "AI Calendar" tile — it carries a "SETUP" badge until you grant calendar access.
Switch between Day and Week with the segmented picker in the toolbar; use "Today" and the arrows either side of the date to move around.
In the "Scheduling AI" sidebar, type into the "Ask AI to schedule..." field and press Return.
Click "+" in the toolbar to add an event by hand, or click any event card to open its detail sheet.

AI Calendar — Works with: Apple Calendar through EventKit — the only source that returns events today
mChatAI's platform memory — every event added here is also written to the shared memory store under a "calendar" namespace

AI Contacts: Apple Contacts with your own favorites, groups and CRM notes, plus AI web research on a person.
Tools · Asks for Contacts permission the first time

AI Contacts — What it does: Reads Apple Contacts, and also derives contacts from calendar event attendees and organisers over a 30-days-back to 30-days-ahead window, adding anyone whose email is not already in Apple Contacts.
An alphabetically sectioned sidebar with search across name, email, company and job title, a Favorites section, a group filter, and a "Birthdays Today" banner you can dismiss until tomorrow.
Favorites, groups and "hidden" flags are your own layer on top of Apple Contacts, stored in CloudKit so they reach the iOS app. Deleting asks whether you mean "Hide from mChatAI" or "Delete from Apple Contacts".

AI Contacts — What it does: When you filter to a group, its banner gets an "Actions" menu: "Message All" opens a compose sheet, "Email All" opens your mail client addressed to every member, and "Export vCard" writes a .vcf of the group to your Desktop and reveals it in Finder.
"AI Actions" → "Research Contact" sends the person's name plus company, job title, location and any non-consumer email domain to a web-search model (Perplexity, falling back to Google) and fills a "Web Presence" section with a short bio and links to whichever LinkedIn, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, GitHub or personal-site profiles it is confident about.

AI Contacts — What it does: Contacts with a company, a job title, or a group with "work" in the name get a "Professional CRM" section: a deal-stage segmented picker, free-text notes, and a next action with an optional due date, all saved per contact as you type.

AI Contacts — How to try it: Expand the "More Apps" band on the home screen and open the "AI Contacts" tile — it carries a "SETUP" badge until you grant contacts access.
Select someone in the sidebar, open the "AI Actions" menu in the toolbar and choose "Research Contact" to fill in the "Web Presence" section.
Right-click a contact row and use "Add to Group", then filter with the groups menu in the toolbar and use the group banner's "Actions" menu for "Email All" or "Export vCard".
AI Contacts — How to try it: Open the gear button in the toolbar for "Contacts Settings" and choose "Import Contacts..." if you would rather sync only the people you pick.

AI Contacts — Works with: Apple Contacts (read, edit and delete)
Apple Calendar — event attendees and organisers become extra contact entries
CloudKit — favorites, groups, hidden flags and web-research results sync to the iOS app
Your mail client, via a mailto link for group email

AI Slides: Describe a deck, approve the outline, then edit the slides, present them, or export a PDF.
Tools

AI Slides — What it does: Two-step generation: you describe the deck and optionally paste source material, get back an outline whose rows you can retitle, reorder, delete, add to and assign a layout, and only then press "Generate Deck" so the slides are written against a skeleton you approved.
Twelve fixed layouts — Title, Section, Bullets, Two Columns, Image Left, Image Right, Full Image, Quote, Big Fact, Chart, Table and Blank. You fill in each layout's own fields and switch layout from a picker; the renderer owns the geometry, so there is no free-form canvas to knock out of alignment.

AI Slides — What it does: A chart or table slide can point at a Ledger collection by name, with a column and a kind (Auto, Bars, Line, Stat, Table). The slide reads live rows out of the Ledger record store when it renders and when it exports.
The right column toggles between "Edit" — per-slide AI buttons, layout, image (choose a file or generate one), Ledger data, background and speaker notes — and "AI", a deck agent you instruct in plain English. The service validates every action the model proposes against the live deck and reports what actually changed, or says "Couldn't apply".

AI Slides — What it does: "Present" opens a full-screen audience window plus a separate presenter window showing the next slide, the speaker notes at an adjustable size and an elapsed timer, driven by arrows, space, B to blank and Esc to end.
Export writes a vector PDF (one page per slide, rendered through the same view the editor draws), PNG images, or Markdown. Slides marked "Skip in show" are excluded, and a failed write throws a real message instead of reporting success.

AI Slides — How to try it: Open the "AI Slides" tile from the "Tools" band on the home screen.
Press "Generate with AI", describe the deck, paste anything useful under "Source material", set the slide count and theme, then press "Draft Outline".
Fix the slide titles, layouts and order on the outline step, then press "Generate Deck".
Use the right column's "AI" tab to change the deck in plain English, then press "Present", or open the "Export" menu and pick "PDF…".

AI Slides — Works with: Ledger — chart and table slides read live rows from a named Ledger collection
Vault — saving a deck registers it as an end product, and slide titles are written into platform memory
Image generation, routed by the applet's own provider picker (Google and mChatAI Cloud map straight through; every other choice falls back to OpenAI)
mchatai-source — the themes and the per-slide AI button wording load from content files, not from the binary

AI ToDo: Task lists that sync to your iPhone, plus a panel that turns one task into a list of subtasks.
Tools

AI ToDo — What it does: Keeps several named lists in a sidebar. Each task carries notes, a priority (Low / Medium / High / Urgent), a status (Pending / In Progress / Blocked / Done), tags and a due date, and anything past its due date is flagged OVERDUE.
Drag a task onto another list in the sidebar to move it there. Filter the current list by All / Active / Done, and sort by Manual, Priority, Due Date, Created or Title — hand reordering by dragging only works while the sort is set to Manual.

AI ToDo — What it does: An "AI Assistant" panel runs four things: Suggest Subtasks, Prioritize Items, Analyze Blockers, Summarize Progress. Only Suggest Subtasks writes back into the list, through an "Add as Tasks" button — the other three return text you read in the panel.

AI ToDo — What it does: Right-clicking a task offers "AI Actions", which hands that task's title and notes as the goal to a coding agent — the buttons read "Dev Agent (Claude)", "Dev Agent (Codex)", "Dev Agent (Gemini)" — or to a built-in "Research Agent", then jumps you to that running session. Buttons you cannot use yet are shown greyed with the reason ("mChatAIShell not connected", "Agent not configured").

AI ToDo — What it does: A bar along the bottom shows done/total and a percentage, and holds a menu with "Remove Done Items" (which sweeps completed tasks into a list called Done Items) and "Delete Done Items". Lists sync over iCloud, and an iCloud button in that same bar forces an immediate push-and-pull.

AI ToDo — How to try it: Open AI ToDo, then click the + beside "Lists" in the sidebar to make a list.
Type into the "Add a new task..." box — it sits just under the All / Active / Done filter bar — and press Enter.
Click the sparkles "AI Assistant" button in the toolbar, run "Suggest Subtasks", then click "Add as Tasks" to keep the results.
Right-click any task and pick "AI Actions" to hand it to a Dev Agent or the Research Agent.

AI ToDo — Works with: The iOS mChatAI app — it has a ToDo applet too, and both read the same CloudKit records
Dev Agent sessions (Claude / Codex / Gemini), which require mChatAIShell to be connected
The built-in Research Agent, which does not require the shell
CLI Portal agent verbs

AI Weather: A weather screen over a live radar map, with saved spots for skiing, surfing, sailing or hiking.
Tools · Asks for Location permission the first time

AI Weather — What it does: Gets the forecast for your current location and falls through three sources in order — NOAA, then Apple WeatherKit, then Open-Meteo — so it keeps working outside the US and without an API key.
Shows current conditions and temperature, a 12-hour hourly strip, wind / humidity / pressure, and a 5-day forecast. Where NOAA has no 5-day coverage it says "5-day forecast unavailable for this location" rather than leaving a hole, and shows placeholder rows while the second call is still in flight.

AI Weather — What it does: Type a place into the search field and it pulls the forecast for that place. Saved spots become one-tap chips across the top, each typed as Skiing, Surfing, Sailing, Hiking or plain Weather, added by dropping a pin on a map under "Edit Locations".
The backdrop is a non-interactive MapKit map centred on you, with your saved pins and a RainViewer radar overlay refreshed on a 10-minute cadence. After two minutes on screen, NASA EPIC full-disk Earth imagery starts cross-fading in and out on a 20-second cycle.

AI Weather — What it does: A separate "Visualizer" sheet gives you a map you can actually move. Pan it anywhere and click "Weather Here" to pull the forecast for that point, which pins the temperature on the map.
Caches the last report so the screen opens with real content instead of a spinner, and shows a small line under the temperature with when it was last updated, falling back to the name of the source that supplied it. Apple Weather attribution is pinned as a footer wherever WeatherKit data may be shown.
AI Weather — What it does: With no location permission at all it falls back to a six-city US overview (New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami, Denver, Seattle).

AI Weather — How to try it: Open AI Weather and allow location access when macOS asks.
Type a place into the "Search weather locations..." field and press Enter.
Open the three-line menu inside the search bar, choose "Edit Locations", search or scroll the map, click "Drop Pin", name it and save it as a Skiing or Hiking spot.
From the same menu choose "Visualizer", move the map, and click "Weather Here".

AI Weather — Works with: Apple WeatherKit, NOAA and Open-Meteo as a three-tier source ladder
RainViewer, for the radar tile overlay
NASA's EPIC imagery API, for the rotating background
The iOS mChatAI app, which has its own AI Weather applet

DreamSnap: Make photos and video from a prompt, or edit your own with painted masks and local sliders.
Tools

DreamSnap — What it does: Two tabs, Photos and Videos. Each shows a grid of everything you have made and a sidebar of actions — Import Photo, Take Photo, Make Photo, Photo Trips on one; Import Video, Take Video, Make Video on the other.
"Make Photo" generates an image from a text prompt via Gemini, OpenAI or Stability, with style chips, a "Browse examples" prompt gallery and an optional attached reference photo. If your chosen provider has no key configured, it quietly tries the others in order and uses the first one that does.

DreamSnap — What it does: The photo editor has six modes: Style Transfer (Van Gogh, Anime, Cyberpunk, Watercolor, Retro, Neon, Sketch or your own prompt), Background, Remove Object, Replace Object, Crop and Auto Adjust. Remove and Replace Object open a mask canvas so you paint over the exact thing you mean.
Auto Adjust is entirely local — eight sliders (Brightness, Contrast, Saturation, Warmth, Sharpness, Highlights, Shadows, Vignette) plus a one-click "Auto Enhance" that runs a Core Image and Vision pass: horizon straightening, exposure, white balance, highlight recovery, noise reduction and sharpening. No AI call, no cost.

DreamSnap — What it does: "Make Video" generates video from a prompt, or animates a still you attach, with a camera-motion style, a duration and an aspect ratio (9:16, 1:1, 16:9), using Google's Veo models — Veo 2 or Veo 3 when you are signed in, or your own Gemini key otherwise. The video editor splits clips at the playhead, deletes clips, applies filters, adjusts brightness/contrast/saturation/warmth/sharpness, and changes playback speed.

DreamSnap — What it does: "Photo Trips" scans the geotagged photos in your Photos library and clusters them into past outings, each listing its stops and photo counts. It needs 3 or more photos within 600m of each other over 10 or more minutes to call something an outing, and tells you plainly when a scan finds nothing and why.

DreamSnap — What it does: "Share" on an edited photo runs a server-side image safety check before the publish sheet will even open — any failure, including a network error, blocks it. What gets published is the prompt plus the image, to a shared prompt gallery other users browse; publishes from a non-admin account land pending review.

DreamSnap — How to try it: Open DreamSnap and click "Make Photo" in the sidebar.
Type a description, pick a style chip, click the round arrow button to generate, then click "Save".
Back on the Photos tab click "Import Photo", choose "Remove Object" in the editor, paint over what you want gone, and click "Generate".
Click "Photo Trips" and click "Allow Access to Photos" to scan your library for past outings.

DreamSnap — Works with: The iOS mChatAI app — DreamSnap exists there and the projects sync through the same CloudKit store
The shared prompt gallery, through a publish sheet with an image-moderation preflight
Apple's Photos library, for the Photo Trips scan
mChatAI Cloud, which changes which Veo models are offered when you are signed in
The AI Wizard / harness — images it generates are written into the DreamSnap library as projects, so they appear in the same gallery, and it can deep-link straight to one

MapGuide: A map for saved places, route planning and workout tracking, plus AI-built tours you can publish.
Tools

MapGuide — What it does: An eight-tab sidebar over a MapKit map — Map, Route Planner, Saved Places, Nearby, Workouts, Tours, Route Chat, Settings — with saved places, discovered places and workout breadcrumbs all drawn on the same map.
Route Planner geocodes a start and destination, returns several route options with trade-off chips, and lets you set travel mode (walking, running, cycling, driving, transit), route type, "Avoid Tolls" and "Avoid Highways". The option you pick is saved to a list of recent routes.
Opening a saved or discovered place and pressing "Directions" draws a route line from your current location to it on the map.

MapGuide — What it does: "Nearby" searches around your location and lists results with the distance to each; right-clicking one offers "Save Place", "Open Website" and "Open Wikipedia".
Tours: "Start a Tour" takes a location, source toggles (Wikipedia, Apple Maps POIs), category filters and a stop count, pulls candidates from both sources and merges duplicates. Stops that came with a Wikipedia summary get a short narration written by a model. You then reorder, edit or add stops in the builder and read through them with "Test Play".

MapGuide — What it does: Tours publish to the Community Hub with an auto-generated map snapshot as the cover and can be unpublished again; "Browse Map Tours" installs tours other people published.
Workouts start from a button on the map, show live distance with Pause and Stop while running, and finished sessions land in a Workout History list with distance, duration and elevation gain.

MapGuide — How to try it: Open the "MapGuide" tile from the "Tools" band on the home screen and allow location access when macOS asks.
Click "Tours" in the sidebar, then "Start a Tour" — pick a location, leave "Wikipedia" and "Apple Maps POIs" on, choose categories, and press "Continue".
In the tour builder, add stops with the search field or "Curate Stops Around Here", then press "Test Play" to step through each stop's narration.
Click "Route Planner", press "New Route", type a destination, press "Calculate Route", pick one of the options and press "Save Route".

MapGuide — Works with: Community Hub — publish, unpublish and install tours
The iOS app — tours and saved places are written to CloudKit by MapGuideStore
Wikipedia and Apple Maps points of interest, as the two tour-stop sources
Deep links from elsewhere in the app: a place recommendation artifact with a coordinate sidecar opens MapGuide centred on that spot with a pin

StoryMaker: A long-form writing tool where the AI edits your prose against a story bible you keep.
Tools

StoryMaker — What it does: Projects hold chapters you write in a full editor. Sidebar tabs switch between Chapters, Outline, Bible and Reports; chapters can be dragged to reorder, renamed, summarised ("Generate Summary") and deleted.
Select a passage and the operations row offers Continue, Add Description, Punch Up Humor, Tighten Prose, Improve Dialogue and Critique. Select nothing and it swaps to the chapter-level three: Beat Check, Pacing, Foreshadowing. You can also type a free-form request into an "Ask the AI anything..." box (Cmd-Return sends it).

StoryMaker — What it does: A persona picker — Story Architect, Line Editor, Voice Coach, Comedy Punch-Up, Continuity Editor, Beta Reader, Copy Editor — changes how every one of those operations is approached.
Results arrive as a word-level diff with Removed and Added marked. You can Accept it, Reject it, keep or reject individual paragraphs, hand-edit the final text, pick between alternatives with "Use This", or write feedback and click "Run Refine Loop". An "Iterative Loop" toggle runs up to 5 evaluate/revise passes and shows the model's own score out of 100 for each pass.

StoryMaker — What it does: A Story Bible holds characters (aliases, voice notes, goals, secrets, archetype, personality, relationships), locations, world rules, a glossary and a style guide. "Extract from Chapters" proposes new entries found in what you have written and you approve them with "Add All to Bible". The assembled bible is injected into the prompt for the writing operations under a STORY BIBLE CONTEXT heading, within a token budget.
Project-level "Continuity Scan" and "Thread Tracker" produce reports listing issues and unresolved plot threads with quoted evidence, each markable Mark Resolved, Dismiss or Reopen.

StoryMaker — What it does: Supporting bits: a stats panel (words, reading time, paragraphs, average sentence length, dialogue ratio) computed locally with no AI call, per-chapter content snapshots with a Revert button, project-wide search on Shift-Cmd-F, an operation log, and export to Markdown or plain text.

StoryMaker — How to try it: Open StoryMaker, click the "New Project" (+) button in the toolbar, type a title and click "Create".
Click "Add Chapter" in the sidebar and write or paste a few paragraphs.
Select a sentence, click "Tighten Prose" in the right-hand panel, then review the diff and click "Accept".
Switch the sidebar to "Bible", click "Extract from Chapters", then "Start Extraction" and "Add All to Bible".

StoryMaker — Works with: The iOS mChatAI app — StoryMaker exists there and the projects sync through the same CloudKit store
The shared applet provider picker (AppletProviderMenu), so operations run on whichever model provider you have configured

Video Recorder: Screen and webcam recording, then an editor that cuts out your ums and dead air.
Tools · Asks for Screen Recording permission the first time

Video Recorder — What it does: Records a whole display or a single window using ScreenCaptureKit, with optional webcam, microphone and computer audio, at 24, 30 or 60 fps. The setup screen states plainly that nothing is uploaded and files stay on your Mac.
While recording, a floating control bar and a draggable webcam bubble sit on top of every app. Their window IDs are passed to the capture filter as exclusions, so they do not appear in the finished video. With the mic on, a live transcript fills in as you talk.

Video Recorder — What it does: The editor transcribes the audio with your choice of engine — "Apple (on-device)", "OpenAI Whisper (your key)" or "mChatAI Cloud" — and shows the words. "Auto-clean" finds filler words and dead air and cuts them. An "AI polish" checkbox has Apple's on-device model re-check each flagged word first, so real words are not cut by mistake; if that call fails, the deterministic result stands unchanged.
Drag a range on the waveform to Delete, Silence, Restore, or Re-record your narration over it. Undo and redo apply throughout, and a "Edits saved automatically" badge sits in the header.

Video Recorder — What it does: Add text boxes with their own on-screen start and end times, auto-caption from the transcript (with an on-device "Add punctuation" pass), record a webcam commentary track over an existing video, and speed the result up to 2x.
Export presets are "YouTube — 16:9", "Reels / Shorts — 9:16", "Square — 1:1" and "Original aspect". The Library tab also has "Import Video…" for footage recorded elsewhere and a one-click "Auto-edit & Export".

Video Recorder — How to try it: Open Video Recorder. If asked, click "Enable Screen Recording" and grant it in System Settings.
Under "What to record", pick a source, then switch on "Face bubble (webcam)" and "Microphone + live transcript".
Click "Start Recording", talk for a minute, then press Stop on the floating control bar.
Switch to the Library tab, open the recording, click "Auto-clean", choose an export preset and click "Export".

Video Recorder — Works with: mChatAI Cloud, as one of the three transcription engines
The product deep-link router — a recording can be opened straight from elsewhere in the app, via ids of the form "aividrec-<uuid>"
mchatai-source content: the filler-word list, silence thresholds and the AI-polish prompt are read from harness/autoedit/autoedit-config.json in the source repo, with clamped fallbacks in the binary, so they can be tuned without a new build

AI Feed: A gallery of the things you've made across the app, with a button that opens each one where it lives.
The platform

AI Feed — What it does: Lists finished products newest-first (up to 200) out of the same vault.sqlite store the Vault applet reads. The screen only reads — nothing is created or edited here — and a link from elsewhere in the app opens straight to one product's detail sheet.
Filter chips across the top: All, Apps, Images, Audio, Video, Documents, Pipelines. A pin button at the right narrows the list to items already pinned.
Each row shows the name, a one-line summary (or the prompt it was built from), its type, a Published or Shared badge, the file size, and when it last changed.

AI Feed — What it does: Clicking a row opens a detail sheet that renders the artifact inline — image, audio player, video, web page, text, slide deck or a Ledger table — through a shared preview registry, so a viewer added for one applet appears on every surface.
The sheet's buttons are chosen by product type: a filled Play / Listen / View / Read, then outlined ones such as "Open in Ledger", "Open in AI Slides", "Open in DreamSnap", "Open in AI Audio" and "Reveal in Finder".

AI Feed — What it does: Text documents and research reports get a separate "Share privately" button that produces an unlisted link — deliberately distinct from publishing to the Hub.
A "Details" section lists size, when it was created, when it was last opened, how many iterations it went through, and any deployment links (clickable).

AI Feed — How to try it: Open AI Feed from the Platform band on the home screen.
If it says "No products yet", make something in another applet first — this screen only shows what already exists.
Click a filter chip such as Apps or Audio to narrow the list.
Click a row to open its detail sheet, then use the filled button at the bottom (Play, Listen, View or Read) or an "Open in …" button.

AI Feed — Works with: Vault (reads the same vault.sqlite store)
Ledger (collections register as records.table products with an "Open in Ledger" action)
AI Harness (its output is written into the same product store)
AI Slides
DreamSnap
Image Studio
Community Hub / Discover publishing
Mini Apps runtime (an installed mini-app previews through the real bridged runtime)

AI Harness: Describe what you want built and it drives a coding agent on your Mac until you have something to run.
The platform

AI Harness — What it does: Starts from a picker of eleven things to build, in three groups — "Interactive Apps & Games" (Mini App, macOS App, Full-Stack App, Unity Game), "Automation & Agents" (Pipeline, AI Agent, Custom Skill, DAG Pipeline) and "Advanced & Infrastructure" (MCP Server, Python Service, Tool Advisory). A tile that needs something installed says so on the tile and shows a padlock: "Requires mChatAI Shell", "Requires Unity 6 Editor installed", "Requires an AI provider API key", "Requires mChatAI Shell + Python". There is also a "Just describe what you want — the wizard will figure out the type" escape hatch.

AI Harness — What it does: Below the picker, suggestion chips are split into "Ready to build" and "Unlock with one setup step", so you can see what will work right now before typing anything.
The screen is three panes: a left rail with "New AI Automation" and a "Products" gallery of finished work, a chat in the middle, and a right pane with Preview, Terminal, Logs and Files tabs.
It runs coding CLIs installed on your machine — Claude Code, Codex or Antigravity. A pill in the toolbar names which one and which model is actually in play (for example "Claude · Opus") rather than saying "default".

AI Harness — What it does: Opening that pill gives you a "Primary AI" picker (Auto (ladder) / Claude / Codex / Antigravity), a model per task for that AI ("Iterating / editing", "Building new", "Auto-fixing"), a free-text box to pass an exact model id straight to the CLI for edits, and a list of what recent runs actually ran on.
A separate menu picks a routing strategy rather than a provider: Best Quality, Lowest Cost, or Manual, each with a tooltip explaining what it does.

AI Harness — What it does: Generated mini-apps are installed and previewed live. You can flip the preview between Mobile (375×812 with a Mobile Safari user agent, so media queries fire) and Desktop (1280×800), pop it into its own window with "Window", use "Capture Screenshot" to snap the current frame as the app's Hub thumbnail, or open the source read-only — which shows a diff against the previous version when one exists.

AI Harness — What it does: Console errors from the live preview are counted in a red chip in the pane header; you can read and copy individual errors, "Clear Errors", or "Drop All Logs into Chat" so the harness fixes them. A separate auto-fix loop also runs on its own, and the stop button halts it as well as the current turn.

AI Harness — What it does: "Iterate" takes a description of a change and produces a clean numbered version (Chess v4 → v5) with the original left untouched; a "Just change the look (re-skin)…" option sits in the same popover. A version-history menu lists every version with its age and offers Open or Rollback.
Finished work can be published to Discover / the Community Hub, and generated images and audio carry their own Regenerate, Share, "Publish to Hub" and "Use as base" buttons alongside "Open in …", "Reveal in Finder" and "Copy Path".

AI Harness — What it does: You can dictate into the composer with the mic, paste or attach an image, use "Capture App Screenshot", and point the session at a working folder (with a recent-folders list).
While a session is generating, the composer swaps to "Type to steer the wizard...": a red stop button cancels just the session you are looking at, and an orange steering button queues your message to redirect the run after the current step, with a "Steering queued" banner you can cancel.

AI Harness — How to try it: Open AI Harness from the Platform band on the home screen.
Pick a tile under "Interactive Apps & Games" — "Mini App" is the one with no setup requirement.
Type what you want in the box at the bottom and press the send arrow.
When the app appears in the right-hand Preview tab, click "Iterate", describe one change, and confirm the new numbered version arrives with the original intact.

AI Harness — Works with: mChatAIShell (gates macOS App, MCP Server and Python Service)
Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity CLIs installed on the machine
Mini Apps gallery (generated apps are installed there)
Community Hub / Discover publishing
Vault and AI Feed (finished work is written into the shared product store)
mchataiDev (an "Open in mchataiDev" button on installed mini-apps)
Xcode ("Open in Xcode") and VS Code ("Open in VS Code") handoffs for macOS-app and full-stack output

For You: Works out what you've been into lately from your own activity on your Mac, and offers a way back in.
The platform

For You — What it does: Builds interest clusters from small activity records other applets write (a liked song, an article read, a finished podcast, a saved place, a completed to-do) over a rolling 30-day window. The clustering is pure deterministic code — no LLM, no network.
Each record is filed under its strongest entity, in this order: artist, then the subject title, then author, then first tag, then genre — so a liked David Bowie track in AI Music and a Bowie page in Wikipedia collapse into one cross-applet cluster.

For You — What it does: Each cluster card under "Your interests" shows a strength bar, a Rising / Steady / Cooling badge, the subjects behind it, chips naming which applets it came from, and a signal count with how long ago.
Writes one suggestion card for each of your top five clusters. Apple's on-device model supplies a short "did you know" fact when it is available and is badged "On-device"; when it isn't, a deterministic template sentence is used and the card carries no badge.

For You — What it does: Card buttons are fixed rules, not model choices: "Make a mix" for a music cluster, "Find audiobook" for a reading or audiobook cluster, "Find a podcast", or "Open <applet name>". A music cluster also gets "Find a podcast" as a second button.
"Make a mix" opens a "New mix" sheet in place — you watch it assemble from your liked songs and Apple Music, use "Play this mix", swipe to remove tracks, then Save — rather than silently creating a playlist.

For You — What it does: "Daily fresh picks" is an explicit switch that is off by default. Turned on, and only once you are signed in and have cloud tokens, it checks the web once a day for genuinely recent items about your topics and shows them under "Fresh from the web"; the screen states only the topic words are sent. A Refresh button forces it.
"Ideas from your activity" shows up to four read-only observations from the always-on cross-applet context agent. This screen renders them; it never triggers new ones.

Ledger: A spreadsheet-like home for typed rows that pipelines, agents and mini-apps can all read and write.
The platform

Ledger — What it does: A sidebar lists your collections with a live row count each; selecting one opens a grid with one column per field and a header showing "N of M rows".
Cells are genuinely typed rather than all text: a number is right-aligned and monospaced, a checkbox is a glyph, a colour shows a swatch. Adding a column lets you pick text, line, number, checkbox, select, multiSelect, date, link, richText or color.

Ledger — What it does: The grid behaves like a spreadsheet — click a cell to select it, type to replace, Enter or double-click to edit, Tab across, arrow keys to move. A value the column cannot accept keeps your text on screen and says it was rejected instead of closing silently.
Columns can be renamed from their own header, sorted ascending or descending, moved left / right / to front, resized by dragging, fitted to contents, and hidden (with a chip showing how many are hidden and a "Show All Columns" item). Rows can be appended, duplicated and deleted.

Ledger — What it does: A Filter box narrows the visible rows; a Table / Chart segmented switch flips the pane to a chart — a line-and-area chart plus n / sum / avg / min / max for a number or date column, a horizontal bar chart of counts for a category column.
Import a CSV or TSV file as a new collection: it keeps the file's column order and infers each column's type (all-numeric becomes number, true/false/yes/no becomes checkbox, ISO dates become date, otherwise text). Export the collection to CSV, copy it as TSV, or paste rows in from the clipboard.

Ledger — What it does: An "Agent" button opens a "Data Agent" panel that takes a plain request like "make a table of…". A globe toggle decides whether it searches the web first — an explicit user choice, not the model's. It writes real typed rows, and every applied change is footnoted under the reply (for example "'Seattle Birds' 0 → 58 rows") so it cannot claim success on a write that did not land.

Ledger — What it does: The agent is limited to four operations — create a collection, add a column, append rows, set one cell — and its column types are checked against an allowed list, so it cannot mint a column you would be unable to edit.
Pipelines append rows through a built-in "Ledger Append" skill, and mini-apps can list collections, read, append and search rows through a permission-gated bridge scoped to that app. Runs accumulate — Monday's rows and Tuesday's rows sit in one collection — rather than overwriting.

Ledger — What it does: Every user collection is registered as a product, so tables show up in AI Feed and the Vault with an "Open in Ledger" action. The product row is only a pointer; viewers read the live table back out of the store.

text:
How it's built — On your machine: mChatAI+ — the main app. UI, applets, your settings, your API keys (stored in the macOS Keychain), pipeline execution, agent runs.
mChatAIShell — a companion helper that lets mChatAI+ build apps and run scripts on your machine. Install it from inside mChatAI+ when you need it.
Pipelines, recipes, and any microservices you create — all run locally. The platform never deploys your code centrally.

How it's built — Across your devices: The macOS app syncs data via iCloud — ToDo items, contacts, vault entries, story projects, chat history. If you're signed into the same iCloud account, they show up everywhere automatically.

How it's built — In the cloud: The mchatai.com side runs only generic, platform-level services:
Sign-in (Firebase Auth)
The Community Hub where you can browse and publish mini-apps
Hosted playable pages for community-shared mini-apps
An optional model catalog refresh
Your prompts, your data, and your content stay on your machine. Nothing is logged centrally unless you explicitly send it (e.g., publish a mini-app to the Hub).

keywords: your data and your code stay on your machine by default.
text: Security & privacy: The short version: your data and your code stay on your machine by default. Nothing leaves it unless you explicitly send it (sign in, publish to the Community Hub, call a cloud LLM that you've configured).

Security & privacy — Secrets and credentials: API keys are stored in the macOS Keychain. They are never written to plaintext files. Pipelines and skills reference them by alias and resolve at call time.
OAuth tokens (Gmail, Calendar, etc.) use the same Keychain storage.

Security & privacy — Sandbox: The main mChatAI+ app runs inside Apple's App Sandbox. It cannot read or write files outside folders you've granted access to, and it cannot run arbitrary commands directly. Anything that needs that level of access goes through mChatAIShell, which only listens on your own machine.

keywords: your key, your provider, direct from the app
text:
Security & privacy — LLM call hygiene: The default for every LLM call is your key, your provider, direct from the app.
Prompts and responses are not logged centrally.
Cost and usage data shown in Quality Intelligence is rolled up locally; it doesn't leave your machine.
Security & privacy — Sign-in: You only need to sign in to mchatai.com if you want to publish to the Community Hub. Sign-in uses Firebase Auth with Apple, Google, or Email.

Security & privacy — Sharing: Mini-app publishing uploads a static playable copy for review. Approved items can appear on mchatai.com so other users can play them. That's all that's published.
Personal data is never shared. Contacts, ToDos, vault contents, and chat history live in your iCloud account, not on mchatai.com.
Developer tools: mChatAI+ ships with a small workbench for extending the platform from inside the app.

Developer tools — SkillForge: In-app editor for writing JavaScript skills. Describe what you want; SkillForge scaffolds the code; you test it inside the editor; save, and it's available to every pipeline and agent. You can also start from a provider template (REST API call with these query params and this auth header) and let the template handle the boilerplate.

Developer tools — Pipeline Builder: The visual editor for pipelines. Drag steps, configure each one's keys, run the pipeline, inspect each step's input and output. Save as a template to schedule it or share it.

Developer tools — DAG Canvas: A node-based editor for non-linear workflows — branching, parallel fan-out, conditional joins. Useful when a pipeline's "next step" depends on what the previous step actually produced.

Developer tools — MCP Studio: Connect to Model Context Protocol servers — the open standard for letting LLMs talk to external tools. Add an MCP server, mChatAI+ discovers its tools, and they show up as callable skills in pipelines, agents, and AI Harness.

Developer tools — Python Microservice Studio: Build small FastAPI microservices in-app. mChatAIShell runs them on your machine; mChatAI+ talks to them through a typed interface, and the platform handles installing, starting, and stopping them transparently.
